lineas.texto: Part Two. You will hear a woman called Ruth Okonjo talking about her work as a cartographer. For each question, complete the sentence with a word or a short phrase.
Hello. My name's Ruth Okonjo, and I'm a cartographer. That's a fancy word for someone who makes maps.
People imagine me out on a hillside with a measuring instrument, but the truth is far less romantic: most of my working day is spent in front of a screen.
I studied geography at university, though what really pushed me towards this career was a module in statistics. I'd expected to hate it, and instead it turned out to be the thing I was best at.
My first job after graduating was with a small publisher that produced walking guides. The pay was terrible. What it gave me, though, was patience.
The hardest part of the job isn't the drawing. It's deciding what to leave out. A map that shows everything is useless, so every map is really an argument about what matters.
These days most of my commissions come from local councils, and increasingly from hospitals, who want maps that a frightened visitor can read in ten seconds.
The mistake beginners make is using too many colours. Three is usually plenty.
If you're thinking of doing this, my advice is simple: learn to draw badly and quickly. The sketch is where the thinking happens.
That is the end of Part Two.
